doc.title: Michael Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 22, 2021

title: 'The last of the truth' and Frank Wess
summary: Weiss explains an old Jazz Times remark: players of earlier generations are unfiltered, as in Frank Wess's phrasing.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: You had a statement from Jazz Times and you said the 60s and 70s age group was the last of the truth. And I’m assuming you’re talking about some of the people like Johnny Griffin you’ve played with, and I’m wondering what you meant by the last of the truth?
Well it was probably a long time ago.
It was quite a while back and you were also commenting on the public’s exposure to mediocre talent. I think it might have been the same article.

Well a lot of things have changed since then. My outlook, the way I think about things have probably changed since then. But yeah. First I think of the players who established themselves in various heydays of the development of this music as the truth because it’s unfiltered, it’s from the horse’s mouth so to speak, and successive younger generations, you know, are reinterpreting and it’s just another filtration system that’s going on. And sometimes — sometimes yes, sometimes not — and again everything comes down to

one’s own idea of good taste but a certain authenticity, a certain way of delivering this language is represented by those players. And you know as they pass on what people now think of what jazz is is left to later generations of how people play these days. And I think there’s so much, there’s so many components to the language of jazz that it developed over the years, over almost a hundred years now. They go through a lot of different transformations and I think that’s what I was trying to express when I said that.
The stylistic changes in that hundred years are quite amazing and I’m wondering if it becomes harder and harder to be innovative and still create music that is listenable and appealing?

You know it’s all up to the music maker, what choices they make. You know I mean we were talking about what you were asking me about before — the last of the truth — I think what came to mind is like the way Frank Wess plays a phrase on his horn. He’s expressing his life experience. My experience and someone in their 30s or in their 20s can’t possibly have that experience to be able to express that way on their horn, what he heard, what he grew up with, what’s in his DNA. That’s what I’m talking about. And you know to be able to play with somebody like that first-hand and experience that is priceless.
